items.title: Trump calls Putin his friend
items.text: US President Donald Trump is defending his recent trilateral summit in China with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, even though the high-profile meeting produced few concrete results and left American allies unsettled . At a news conference on Friday, Trump described Putin as his friend and insisted that their personal relationship could help end Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine. However, Trump declined to say whether Putin acts as a friend to American interests. He stated that ending the conflict is extremely difficult and blamed both sides for not knowing how to stop it. Shortly after the summit, Trump also called into a meeting of European leaders and reportedly questioned their continued support for Ukraine, right as fresh Russian strikes damaged European embassies in Kyiv. Despite Trump’s claims of progress, analysts note that Putin has shown no sign of wanting peace and no peace deal is any closer. Difficult words: trilateral (involving three groups, parties, or countries), unsettled (anxious, uneasy, or worried about a situation), decline (to refuse to accept, do, or answer something). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Trump calls Putin his friend
items.text: US President Donald Trump is defending his recent meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. Although the meeting brought together the world’s three biggest powers, it achieved very few real results and worried America’s European allies . At a news conference on Friday, Trump called Putin his friend and said their good relationship could help stop the war in Ukraine. Trump could not say if Putin is a friend to the United States, though. Soon after the meeting, Trump spoke to European leaders and questioned why they continue to support Ukraine, even as new Russian attacks hit buildings in Kyiv. Critics point out that Putin started the invasion and shows no real signs of stopping the war, which means Trump is still far from making a peace deal. Difficult words: ally (a country or organization that formally cooperates with and supports another, especially in politics or war), question (to express doubt about something, or to ask someone questions to get information), invasion (coming to a country or region with an armed force). items.title: Trump calls Putin his friend
items.text: US President Donald Trump meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. The big meeting does not bring many real results . It makes America’s friends in Europe feel worried. On Friday, Trump calls Putin his friend. He says that their good relationship can help end the war in Ukraine. But Trump does not say if Putin is good for America. Later, Trump talks to European leaders. He asks why they still help Ukraine. At the same time, Russia attacks Kyiv again. Many people say that Putin does not want to stop fighting. There is still no peace deal . Difficult words: result (how a situation ends), relationship (how two or more people, groups, or countries behave toward each other), peace deal (a formal deal between countries to stop fighting). items.title: Runners and cyclists make art
items.text: Fitness fanatics are creating art while tracking their runs and bike rides on their phones, turning their exercise into a masterpiece. When you create art with your GPS as a paintbrush, you follow points on a map to make a single line across an area to create the art. You enter the points into a fitness tracking app called Strava in advance , and the app then traces your every move. If you make a mistake, your whole artwork has to be started all over again. Artists from around the world upload their drawings to Instagram, where they join a growing gallery with more than 18,000 pieces posted under the hashtag GPS Art that already show hundreds of thousands of kilometers. Artists say that the activity is a mix of art and exercise, and for many, it began with the pandemic when traffic suddenly went away and people had more free time. Difficult words: fanatic (a person who’s extremely interested in something), in advance (before doing a particular thing), hashtag (the symbol # that’s used on social media to describe the general subject). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Runners and cyclists make art
items.text: During the coronavirus pandemic, there were fewer cars on the roads, and people had more free time, too. Some runners and cyclists started to create new and unusual art. Strava is a GPS cycling and running app, and some people started to use it as a paintbrush to create art. They entered some points in the app, and then they followed the points to make a line from them. Cyclists sometimes went tens of kilometers because if they made a mistake, they had to start all over again. The result is amazing. People make symbols, pictures, or even messages which they can share with other people on social media. One Instagram gallery already had more than 18,000 pieces of art, and people from all the world add theirs every day. Many people enjoyed this activity because it was a good way to exercise and create art at the same time. Difficult words: GPS (an electronic system which uses satellites to tell where exactly someone or something is), enter (to put data or information into a computer), gallery (a place where people see and sometimes can buy works of art). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Runners and cyclists make art
items.text: Some runners and cyclists have a new hobby . They make special art . Fewer cars are on the roads during the coronavirus. People also have more free time. Some people make pictures. They use the Strava app . Strava is a cycling and running app. It shows where someone runs or cycles. Some people plan where they go. They put points in the app. Then they run or cycle. They connect the points. They make a picture from the points. They must start again if they make a mistake. One gallery on the Internet already has more than 18,000 pictures. People from all the world put the pictures there. There are new pictures every day. Difficult words: hobby (an activity which someone does in his free time for fun), art (paintings, drawings, music, and so on), app (a computer program in a mobile phone which does special things), gallery (a place to show art). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: U.S. brings an end to production of one-cent coin
items.text: The United States has officially brought an end to the production of its one-cent coin. President Donald Trump signed the Common Cents Act on Friday. However, the coin will remain legal tender and continue circulating. The US Mint had actually stopped manufacturing the penny (the nickname for the coin) in November 2025. Businesses now have to round cash transactions up or down to the nearest five cents when exact change is unavailable. The decision to discontinue minting the penny was an economic one. In 2024, each coin cost 3.69 cents to produce. The bill's author, Lisa McClain, said: "This legislation will save $85 million per year by permanently ending penny production. It's common sense." The penny's history dates back to the founding years of the United States. Congress established the US Mint in 1792. The following year, the mint distributed more than 11,000 one-cent coins. The penny underwent numerous design changes. Early designs included an image of Liberty, a Native American chief's headdress, and an eagle. In 1909, it featured a portrait of former President Abraham Lincoln to commemorate the centenary of his birth. The last major redesign was in 2010. Rising manufacturing costs gradually undermined the coin's viability, consigning it to history. items.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is released worldwide
items.text: Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) has finally been released. Millions of video game fans worldwide are now playing it. They have waited 13 years for a new GTA game since the release of GTA 5. Gaming experts say the latest version could be the biggest entertainment release in history. It has already sold millions of copies, and it is set to make billions of dollars. Some fans are so excited that they are taking days off work or school to play it. An HR company in the UK said that workers in Britain booked around 83,000 days off because of the game. Many fans tried to make their games consoles think they lived in New Zealand by changing their region settings. They tried this so they could play the game earlier. GTA 6 has received excellent reviews for its high-quality, realistic graphics and exciting story. Players get to explore a huge world of crime and follow the lives of two criminals. However, many experts warn that the game is unsuitable for children under the age of 17. That is because it contains violence, killing, car theft, bad language, drugs, alcohol and sexual content. Media expert Jasmine Hood Miller said: "In GTA, players commit crimes, sometimes against ordinary people who did nothing wrong." She added: "GTA is a very well-made game that teens find fun to play." items.title: Wire upgrade at fault for grounding all US flights
items.text: Thousands of flights across the USA were grounded on Friday the 13th following a major communications failure in the country's air traffic control system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop after problems with radar and communications equipment. More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Thousands of flights were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded at airports nationwide. The problem was eventually traced to an overloaded router, possibly as a result of maintenance work to replace decades-old copper wires with fibre-optic cables. The FAA lifted the ground stop almost five hours later. Operations may take days to return to normal. The incident sparked widespread concern. Officials quickly reassured the public that it was not another 9/11. The US homeland security secretary said there had been no indication of a cyberattack or national security threat. He described the incident as a "telecommunications outage". Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the failure on outdated infrastructure. He said: "We have old switches and old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines." He added: "It's an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded." Duffy warned that systems would "continue to break" unless Congress allocated extra funds. He said: "I can't build things if I don't have money." items.title: France blames Iran for cyberattack on freezers
items.text: The French government has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket freezers and refrigerators across France. The attacks happened last month. They hit around 700 supermarkets and shops. Hackers took control of the cooling systems in the fridges and freezers. Temperatures increased to more than 50 degrees Celsius. Thousands of tons of frozen food melted. Stores had to throw the food away because it was no longer safe to eat. The French Foreign Minister said the attack was on a level never seen before. France believes an Iranian cyber unit carried out the attack. Iran has strongly denied it was involved in the attacks and blamed the French government for them. Security experts have warned that cyberattacks could be more dangerous in the future. Similar attacks have already affected other European countries. A French blood bank has also been hit. Fortunately, workers stopped the blood products from being damaged. Cybersecurity expert Gerome Billois stated: "At the moment, they are attacking easy equipment, but we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity." Weak computer security can let hackers attack places and services, such as hospitals, airports, public transport and banks. This can put people's lives in danger. European officials have said that a strong response is needed. Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Oil pollution in the sea
items.text: Severe oil pollution from damaged ships during the conflict involving Iran is threatening marine life and coastal communities across the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. According to the International Maritime Organization, 136 maritime incidents have been confirmed in the region, while Greenpeace reports that satellite monitoring has detected more than 500 oil slicks since the war began. One recently spotted slick covers around 300 square kilometers, including a thick, dark section of heavy oil. Environmental experts warn that because the Gulf consists of shallow, semi-enclosed waters with limited exchange with the open ocean, trapped oil can remain in the environment for years. The spills have already washed onto coastlines in Iran, Oman, and the United Arab Emirates, and some beaches had to be closed temporarily. Conservationists are deeply concerned about vulnerable marine habitats , coral reefs, and rare species such as sea turtles and the endangered Arabian Sea humpback whale. Difficult words: slick (a film or layer of oil floating on water, especially one that has leaked from a ship), semi-enclosed (partially surrounded or shut in by land or barriers, limiting connection to the open sea), habitat (the natural home or environment of an animal, plant, or other organism). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Oil pollution in the sea
items.text: Oil leaking from damaged ships during the war with Iran is causing serious damage in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. International officials confirmed 136 ship incidents in the area, and Greenpeace found more than 500 oil spills using satellite photos. One huge oil spill covers about 300 square kilometers of water. Experts explain that because the Gulf is shallow and mostly closed off from the open ocean, the dangerous oil stays in the water for a very long time. Oil already reached beaches in Iran, Oman, and the United Arab Emirates, and some beaches had to close. This pollution is a major threat to coral reefs, coastal towns, and rare sea animals, including sea turtles and whales. Difficult words: shallow (not deep), threat (a person or thing likely to cause damage or danger), pollution (harmful substances in water, air, or soil). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Oil pollution in the sea
items.text: Damaged ships from the war near Iran are leaking a lot of oil into the sea. Space photos show more than 500 areas of oil on the water. Because this part of the sea is not very deep , the dirty oil stays there for a long time. Oil is already on beaches in Iran, Oman, and the United Arab Emirates. Some beaches must close. This is very bad for people who live near the sea and for ocean animals. Whales, sea turtles, and coral reefs are now in great danger because of the oil. Difficult words: d amaged (broken or hurt), leak (when liquid or gas gets out from a place into water or air), deep (when there is not much water under you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: India has too much rice
items.text: Thanks to modern plant science and generous government subsidies , India has become one of the world’s largest rice producers. Decades ago, India struggled to feed its population, so the government introduced guaranteed minimum prices, and scientists created new rice plants that survive heavy floods. As a result, India’s annual rice production has grown by 50 percent in ten years, which created a massive surplus that makes up 40 percent of global rice exports. However, this big success is now causing serious financial and political problems. Warehouses are overflowing, and the government spends over 24 billion dollars a year on food subsidies. This means Indian taxpayers are effectively paying for cheap food sold abroad. Rival countries like the United States and Thailand complain that India’s cheap exports hurt their own farmers. Meanwhile, growing so much rice strains groundwater supplies and leaves less land for other essential crops like oilseeds and pulses. Yet politicians remain reluctant to cut farmer bonuses because they fear losing rural votes. Difficult words: subsidy (money paid by a government or organization to help keep the price of a product or service low, or to support an industry like farming), surplus (an amount of something more than what is needed or used), reluctant (unwilling and hesitant). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: India has too much rice
items.text: Thanks to modern science and strong government financial support, India has become the world’s top rice producer. Sixty years ago, the country struggled with food shortages , but new flood-resistant rice seeds and guaranteed farmer payments help rice grow far beyond what India’s people can eat. Today, Indian rice makes up 40 percent of the world market, but this big success is causing serious problems. Storage buildings are full, and the government spends billions of dollars on farm subsidies . But it is losing money importing other needed foods. Other countries, such as the United States and Thailand, also complain that India sells its rice too cheaply and hurts their farmers. Even though growing too much rice uses up underground water, local leaders are afraid to reduce farmer bonuses because they want to win elections. Difficult words: shortage (when there is not enough of something what people need), guarantee (to promise formally that something will happen), subsidy (financial help to farmers or businesses). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: India has too much rice
items.text: India now grows more rice than its people can eat. Sixty years ago, India does not have enough food. The government gives farmers money to grow more rice. Also, scientists make stronger plants. Today, India sells a lot of rice to other countries. But this big success is causing new problems. Storage rooms are full of extra rice. The government gives very much money to helping farmers. Other countries like the United States and Thailand are angry. Indian rice is too cheap . Growing so much rice also uses too much water. But leaders do not want to stop paying farmers because they need to be friends with them. Difficult words: success (when you are good at something, or achieve something special), storage room (a room where we keep products or food), cheap (when something costs very little money). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Nails on roads
items.text: Ontario police officers in West Nipissing, Canada, are currently investigating multiple reports of roofing nails being deliberately dumped onto local roads and highways. Authorities warn that these scattered nails pose a serious safety hazard to drivers, as they can trigger sudden tire blowouts and cause motorists to lose control of their vehicles at high speeds. Beyond the immediate risk of dangerous road accidents, drivers also face unexpected financial costs from having to repair or replace punctured tires. Because the incidents appear to be intentional acts of vandalism or endangerment, investigators are treating the matter with urgency and working to identify those responsible. Police are urging residents, commuters, and anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity along the affected routes or who has relevant dashcam footage or information regarding previous incidents to come forward and contact police immediately. Difficult words: blowout (a sudden loss of air pressure from a tire while driving), vandalism (deliberate destruction of or damage to public or private property), suspicious (seeming to involve criminality or wrongdoing). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Nails on roads
items.text: Police in a town in Canada are investigating reports that someone is purposely throwing roofing nails onto local roads and highways. Officers warn drivers that these sharp nails are a major safety danger because they can cause sudden flat tires and make drivers lose control of their cars. Also, damaged tires cost drivers a lot of money to repair or replace. Investigators believe the nails were left on the roads purposely and are trying to find out who did it. Police are asking anyone who saw someone dumping nails or has helpful information about past incidents to call them right away so they can keep the roads safe for everyone. Difficult words: purposely (done with a plan or doing it rather than by accident or mistake), roofing nail (a short nail used mainly for constructing roofs), dump (to drop something in a careless or untidy way). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
